Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether a real operator on $L_2(\mathbb{R})$ with all real eigenvalues and a basis of eigenvectors can have a single eigenvalue with infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors.

**Answer: Yes.**

## Proof

The key observation is that $L_2(\mathbb{R})$ is an **infinite-dimensional** Hilbert space, so there is no finite upper bound on the dimension of any eigenspace $\ker(\phi - \lambda I)$. We construct an explicit example.

**Construction.** Let $\{h_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}$ be the Hermite functions, which form a complete orthonormal basis for $L_2(\mathbb{R})$ (each $h_n$ is real-valued). Define $\phi : L_2(\mathbb{R}) \to L_2(\mathbb{R})$ on the basis by:

$$\phi(h_n) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}, \\ \dfrac{1}{n+1} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}, \end{cases}$$

and extend by linearity and continuity. Since the eigenvalues $\{0\} \cup \{1/(n+1) : n \text{ odd}\}$ all lie in $[0, \tfrac{1}{2}]$, the operator is bounded with $\|\phi\| = \tfrac{1}{2}$, hence $\phi$ is a well-defined bounded linear operator on $L_2(\mathbb{R})$.

**Verification of the three required properties:**

1. **All eigenvalues are real.** The spectrum of eigenvalues is $\left\{0,\, \tfrac{1}{2},\, \tfrac{1}{4},\, \tfrac{1}{6},\, \dots\right\}$, every element of which is real. ✓

2. **The set of eigenvectors forms a basis for $L_2(\mathbb{R})$.** Every Hermite function $h_n$ is an eigenvector: $\phi(h_n) = \lambda_n h_n$ with $\lambda_n \in \{0\} \cup \{1/(n+1): n \text{ odd}\}$. The collection $\{h_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $L_2(\mathbb{R})$. ✓

3. **A single eigenvalue has infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors.** The eigenvalue $\lambda = 0$ has eigenvectors $\{h_0, h_2, h_4, h_6, \dots\}$, i.e., all even-indexed Hermite functions. This is an **infinite** set of mutually orthogonal (hence linearly independent) eigenvectors, all corresponding to the single eigenvalue $0$. ✓

**Why this is possible.** In a finite-dimensional space of dimension $d$, the eigenspace for any eigenvalue has dimension at most $d$, so the number of linearly independent eigenvectors for a single eigenvalue is bounded by $d$. In the infinite-dimensional space $L_2(\mathbb{R})$, no such bound exists. The eigenspace $\ker(\phi - \lambda I)$ can be any closed subspace—finite or infinite dimensional. In our construction, $\ker(\phi)$ is the closed linear span of $\{h_{2k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$, an infinite-dimensional subspace, yielding infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors for the single eigenvalue $0$.

**Even simpler example.** The identity operator $I$ on $L_2(\mathbb{R})$ has the single eigenvalue $1$, every vector is an eigenvector, and any orthonormal basis of $L_2(\mathbb{R})$ is a basis of eigenvectors—giving infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors for the eigenvalue $1$.

**Conclusion.** There is no obstruction in infinite dimensions to a single eigenvalue possessing infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors. The construction above (and the trivial identity example) confirms that a real operator $\phi : L_2(\mathbb{R}) \to L_2(\mathbb{R})$ with all real eigenvalues and a basis of eigenvectors **can** have infinitely many linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to a single eigenvalue.
